notes.b: Freezing preserves food by lowering its temperature far enough to stop enzyme action and microbial growth, and by turning free water into ice that micro-organisms cannot use. It is popular because no high heat is needed, so food stays close to fresh.
points: Low temperature slows enzyme reactions (enzymes are the natural chemicals in food that make it spoil or change) and stops micro-organisms from reproducing, but it does not kill most of them.
Frozen food is not sterile: micro-organisms become dormant (inactive) and start growing again when the food thaws, so frozen food is never safe indefinitely.
Turning free water into ice removes the water micro-organisms need, because ice is unavailable to them.
Pure water freezes at 0 °C, but food freezes below this because its dissolved sugars and salts lower its freezing point.
Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes, which is why liquids need headspace (an empty gap at the top) in their containers.

Freezing itself does little harm to nutritive value, and colour, flavour and texture are kept better than with most other methods because no high heat is used, except in blanching; most nutrient losses happen during blanching and thawing.
notes.tip: Never write that freezing sterilises food or kills micro-organisms. Say they are inactivated (dormant) and the water is unavailable to them, and that they can grow again after thawing.

notes.b: The speed of freezing decides how big the ice crystals are, and crystal size decides how much damage the food suffers. Quick freezing makes small crystals; slow freezing makes large ones.
points: Quick freezing takes place at about −25 °C (the 2013 Higher Level scheme gives −25 °C to −40 °C) in the fast-freeze section of a freezer, so the food passes through the freezing range rapidly.
Quick freezing forms small ice crystals within the cells, which causes little damage to the cell walls, so there is little drip (juice lost) on thawing.
For this reason quick freezing retains the texture, colour, flavour and nutritive value of food better than slow freezing does.
Slow freezing takes place at a higher temperature than −25 °C, as in an ordinary freezer compartment, where ice forms gradually.
Slow freezing forms large ice crystals, mostly between the cells, that pierce and rupture cell walls, allowing juices to escape.
As a result slow-frozen food is limp and soft when thawed, and it loses colour and flavour and drip containing soluble vitamins B1 and C and minerals.
The fast-freeze setting should be switched on about 3 to 4 hours before food is placed in the freezer, so the freezer is cold enough to freeze the new food quickly.
Diagram: draw two cells side by side, one with small crystals inside an intact cell wall (quick) and one with large crystals and a ruptured wall (slow).
notes.tip: Quick means small crystals and slow means large crystals; exam traps reverse them, so check your wording. Give the temperature (−25 °C), crystal size, effect on cell walls, effect on texture, colour, flavour and nutrients, and drip loss.

notes.b: Blanching is a brief heat treatment given to vegetables before freezing. Enzymes keep working slowly even at freezer temperatures, so vegetables would spoil in storage without it.
points: 1. The vegetables are plunged into boiling water for a short, set time that depends on the vegetable.
2. They are plunged immediately into ice-cold water for the same length of time, which stops the cooking so the vegetables do not go soft.
3. They are drained and dried, because surface water left on them would form ice crystals.
Blanching inactivates enzymes that would otherwise cause loss of colour, flavour, texture and nutrients during frozen storage.
Blanching also cleans the vegetable, destroys some micro-organisms on its surface, softens it slightly so it packs well, and keeps its bright colour.

Blanching loses some water-soluble vitamins, particularly vitamin C and vitamin B1, into the water and through heat. Blanch small batches in plenty of fast-boiling water so the water returns to the boil quickly and the timing stays short and accurate.
Fruit is not blanched; soft fruit is open-frozen on trays or packed in sugar or sugar syrup. Some foods, such as soups, sauces and casseroles, are frozen cooked after cooling.
notes.tip: Blanching is for vegetables, not fruit, and its purpose is to inactivate enzymes, not to cook the vegetable. Give the method (boiling water, then ice-cold water for the same time) and the loss of vitamins C and B1.

notes.b: Good results at home depend on following a set of steps, and each step has a reason. Most of them aim either to freeze the food quickly or to keep air and moisture away from it.
points: Choose fresh, best-quality food in perfect condition and freeze it soon after harvest or purchase, because freezing keeps quality but cannot improve it. Wash, peel, trim or cut as needed, blanch vegetables, and cool cooked food quickly before it goes into the freezer.
Portion food into usable (family-sized) quantities so that only what is needed is thawed.

Open-freeze (tray-freeze) sticky or delicate items, such as strawberries or raspberries, or items to be kept separate, such as sausages and burgers: spread them in a single layer on a tray, freeze hard, then bag them so that they stay separate.

Pack food in strong, moisture-proof and vapour-proof freezer bags, foil or rigid plastic containers, and remove as much air as possible so that the food does not dry out. Leave headspace in containers holding liquids to allow for expansion as the food freezes.

Seal tightly and label with contents and date. Place new packs against the cold surfaces or in the fast-freeze compartment, as the freezer instructs, and keep them apart from already frozen food until frozen, so they freeze quickly.
Do not overload the freezer: freeze no more than about one-tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24 hours, because overloading raises the temperature and slows freezing.

Store frozen food at −18 °C or colder, using the oldest first. The safe storage time depends on the food: fatty foods and oily fish keep for a shorter period, and fatty foods stored too long can turn rancid.
Foods that freeze well include peas, beans, carrots, broccoli, apples, strawberries, meat, fish, bread, cakes, soups, sauces and prepared meals.

Foods that freeze poorly include lettuce, whole tomatoes and other high-water salad foods, bananas, melons, pears, whole eggs in the shell, low-fat cream and mayonnaise-based foods, which go limp, watery or separate.
notes.tip: Tie each rule to its reason when you answer guideline questions: fast freeze 3 to 4 hours ahead, no more than one-tenth of capacity, usable portions, cool first, blanch vegetables, airtight packaging, label and date, store at −18 °C. Quick freezing at −25 °C is the freezing step and −18 °C is storage; do not mix them.

notes.h: Freezer burn, thawing and freezer faults
notes.b: Problems with frozen food usually come from air reaching it or from careless thawing. Both are preventable.
points: Freezer burn shows as dry, discoloured, tough patches where air has reached the surface of the food, caused by dehydration and oxidation, especially in protein foods such as meat and fish.
Airtight packaging with the air removed prevents freezer burn.

Thaw food in a fridge, or cook it from frozen where the food allows, such as vegetables, so that the food stays below the danger zone while it thaws. Thaw meat and poultry fully before cooking unless the pack says otherwise.

Thawed food should be used promptly and not refrozen as it is, because quality declines and micro-organisms may have multiplied. Raw food thawed in the fridge can be cooked and then frozen as a cooked dish.
In a freezer fault or power cut, keep the door closed and do not open it, because frozen food keeps for a time if the cold is held in.
notes.tip: Vitamin B1 and C losses come from blanching, from slow freezing and drip on thawing, and from not cooking vegetables from frozen; mention these if asked how the losses occur.

notes.b: Commercial freezing is faster and colder than home freezing, so ice crystals are smaller and quality is higher. Food is frozen soon after harvesting or catching, often on the farm or on a factory ship. Home freezers are not as cold or as fast, so home freezing does not match these methods.
points: Air blast freezing: a very cold air stream at about −30 °C is blown over food, often on a conveyor belt or through a tunnel; suitable for most foods, such as fruit, vegetables, meat and bakery products.
Plate (contact) freezing: food is pressed between two hollow metal plates cooled by refrigerant; suitable for thin, flat foods such as fish fillets, flat pieces of meat and burgers.

Flow (fluidised bed) freezing: cold air is blown up through a perforated conveyor belt so that small pieces float and freeze individually, staying free-flowing and not sticking together; suitable for peas, sweetcorn and berries.

Cryogenic freezing: food is exposed to liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide at extremely low temperature, which freezes it almost instantly; suitable for delicate or high-value foods such as strawberries, prawns and fish.
The cold chain keeps frozen food at −18 °C or colder in cold stores, refrigerated lorries and supermarket freezer cabinets until it reaches the home.
When buying frozen food, check that the pack is intact with no ice crystals or frost inside, that it is below the load line on the cabinet, and take it home quickly in a cool bag.
notes.tip: Commercial-method questions ask you to name methods with a suitable food each: plate and flow for flat meat and fish and for peas, blast for fruit and vegetables, cryogenic for delicate foods such as strawberries and prawns. Air blast freezing on a conveyor belt is an accepted commercial alternative in a freezing-vegetables account.

notes.b: Freezing helps a household plan meals, save money and cut waste. These benefits are the points examiners expect when they ask about frozen foods in meal planning.
points: Freezing surplus food before it spoils reduces household waste, and leftovers can be frozen for reuse as ready-made portions.
Bulk cooking and freezing portions saves time and fuel, since a large batch is cooked once.
A freezer stock of meals and ingredients provides emergency food and convenience on busy days, including for households with different eating times.
Buying in bulk or when produce is in season is more economical, and freezing keeps it for a longer period (a longer shelf life).
Frozen foods provide a wide variety of vegetables, fish and fruit all year, including items not available fresh locally.

Freezing retains colour, texture, flavour and nutritive value well compared with heat processing; frozen vegetables keep more vitamin C than canned ones, as one past-paper table shows for peas (25 mg fresh, 17 mg frozen, 8 mg canned).
Fruit and salad foods go soft after thawing because of cell damage, so they suit cooking better than eating raw.
Labelling each pack with contents, date and portion size lets older items be used first, which helps planned menus.
notes.tip: For benefits of frozen foods, give separate points with a reason each: waste, time, fuel, emergency stock, shelf life, economy, convenience and variety.

keyTerms.definition: Freezing food rapidly at about −25 °C to −40 °C so that small ice crystals form and cell damage is minimised.
Freezing food at a higher temperature so that large ice crystals form and damage the cell walls.
Briefly boiling vegetables and then cooling them in iced water to inactivate enzymes before freezing.
Dehydration, oxidation and toughening of the surface of frozen food where air has reached it.
Liquid lost from food on thawing, carrying water-soluble vitamins and minerals with it.
The empty space left at the top of a container so that liquid can expand as it freezes.
Commercial freezing in which very cold air is blown over food on a conveyor belt.
Commercial freezing in which cold air blown up through a perforated belt freezes each piece separately so they do not stick together.
Commercial freezing using liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide, which freezes food almost instantly.
Commercial freezing in which food is pressed between two cold metal plates.

factCards.definition: Large ice crystals damage the cell walls, so the food loses texture; colour and flavour are poorer on thawing; soluble vitamins B1 and C are lost in drip.
About −25 °C to −40 °C, in the fast-freeze section of the freezer.

factCards.term: Three things blanching does to vegetables
factCards.definition: It inactivates enzymes, destroys some surface micro-organisms and helps retain colour, flavour and texture during frozen storage.
Air blast freezing, plate (contact) freezing, flow (fluidised bed) freezing and cryogenic freezing.

factCards.term: Four packing guidelines for home freezing
factCards.definition: Use moisture-proof and vapour-proof packaging, remove the air, leave headspace for liquids, and seal, label and date each pack.

factCards.term: Three benefits of frozen food in meal planning
factCards.definition: It reduces waste, saves time and fuel through bulk cooking, and provides emergency stock and convenience.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between quick freezing and slow freezing in terms of ice crystal size and the effect on the food.
questions.model: Quick freezing takes place at about −25 °C to −40 °C, so small ice crystals form within the cells, causing little damage to the cell walls. The food keeps its texture, colour, flavour and nutrients on thawing. Slow freezing takes place at about 0 °C to −24 °C, so large ice crystals form, rupturing cell walls. On thawing the food is soft, loses juice and drip, and loses colour, flavour and nutrients.

questions.prompt: Describe how to carry out home freezing of fresh vegetables, including the preparation, packing and storage, and explain the principle on which freezing preserves them.
questions.model: Principle: low temperature stops enzyme action and microbial growth; water becomes ice and is unavailable to micro-organisms; quick freezing keeps the structure of the food intact. Preparation: choose fresh, best-quality vegetables and blanch them in boiling water for a set time, then cool them rapidly in iced water to inactivate enzymes. Packing: drain and dry, portion into usable quantities, remove as much air as possible in moisture-proof and vapour-proof bags or containers, seal and label with contents and date. Freezing: place packs against the cold walls of the freezer, freezing no more than one-tenth of the capacity in 24 hours, at about −25 °C. Storage: keep at −18 °C or colder and use promptly after thawing.
